5f0c22aacac31c0769f555f9d8231109.text: Seven trustees have been elected or acclaimed to the School District 27 board of education, according to preliminary results from the Oct. 17 elections. Voters have chosen their school trustees for Cariboo-Chilcotin School District 27 following the Oct. 17 election. Fourteen candidates filed nominations for the board’s seven seats. Three trustees were elected by acclamation and the remaining four seats were decided by voters. William Shepherd of 108 Mile Ranch was acclaimed in Zone 2, while incumbent Michael Franklin and Jenny Philbrick, both of Williams Lake, were acclaimed in zones 6 and 7, respectively. Michael Henshall, representing 100 Mile House, won Zone 3 with 345 votes receiving 60.3 per cent of the vote over current board member Camille Macdonald of 70 Mile House. Mary Forbes of Williams Lake, a longtime trustee and the board’s current vice-chair, was re-elected for Zone 5 with 280 votes receiving 64.1 per cent of the vote. For Zone 1, Ella Brown (Elizabeth) got elected with 230 votes receiving 30.8 per cent of the vote, while incumbant Melissa Coates, who joined the board after winning a local by-election in June 2025 was re-elected for Zone 4 with 83 votes receiving 79.8 per cent of the vote. A total of 1,860 ballots were cast across the district in the school trustee election. These results are preliminary and subject to confirmation by the chief election officer. Official results must be declared by 4 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 21.

Williams Lake got the early lead with three goals whereas the Bruins scored one. In the second period, the Mustangs added two more while the Bruins got one. In the third, the Bruins scored one consolation goal and the Mustangs didn’t add anything to the total. Williams Lake held for a 5-3 win. Five different players scored for the Mustangs, with Declan Pocock recording a goal and two assists in the 5-3 win. Pocock was named first star of the game while Nolan Phare was selected as the third star for his defensive zone presence . The Mustangs won the home game by 6-4 against the Princeton Posse. The Posse took a 2-1 lead in the first period, scoring twice before the Mustangs got one back. In the second, the Mustangs cameback with three unanswered goals before Princeton scored one after. In the third, Princeton added one but the Mustangs were able to hold their two goal lead. Matthew Hufty got the Mustangs on the board in the first period. Tristan Aidoo, Brayden Bolt and Aidoo again scored in the second period. During the third, Blake Collison and Braden Bolt scored each goal. Netminder Ivan Anderson made 25 saves on 29 shots for the Mustangs. Blake Collison earned top honours of the night for creating prime scoring opportunities while Tristan Aidoo named second star was recognized for his crucial plays on the ice. 80dce98f34af82fbfd3ea4b60b7f2727.text: Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor was at home Saturday, Oct 17 where he anxiously awaited election results. Preliminary results from this year's municipal election in Williams Lake. Official results won't be declared until Wednesday, Oct. 21. Also at home Saturday, Oct. 17 was former mayor and challenger Walter Cobb where he too awaited election results. Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor will remain mayor of Williams Lake for a second term following this year’s municipal election. According to preliminary results that were shared approximately 50 minutes after voting closed 8 p.m. at Marie Sharpe Elementary School, Rathor was identified as the successful candidate against challenger and former mayor Walt Cobb. Rathor was elected mayor in 2022 after serving as a city councillor for more than 20 years. Rathor was at home with family, friends and supporters eagerly awaiting for the results to come in, shortly after which he shared a Facebook post. “Thank you for trusting me to continue serving as your mayor. To my wife, family, campaign team and this incredible community thank you for believing in me,” he wrote. “I’m honoured, grateful and ready to keep working for you. Together we can!” In 2014 and 2018 Rathor was defeated by Cobb for the top position. Preliminary results which won’t be made official until Wednesday, Oct. 21, show Rathor securing 2,116 votes (913 advance and 1,203 general) compared to Cobb’s total of 1,026 (530 advance and 496 general). Councillor incumbents Scott Nelson and Michael Moses were also successfully re-elected. New faces set to take up a councillor seat include Ruth Lloyd and Nathan Wiebe with past city councillors Jason Ryll and Paul French returning. City of Williams Lake chief election officer Ross Coupé said there were a total of 3,182 ballots cast. Preliminary results show incumbent Sheila Boehm unsuccessful in her re-election efforts. Coun. Joan Flaspohler, Jazmyn Lyons and Angie Delainey did not seek re-election.

f070aa4c7343b3777d943d3c09045d35.text: BC Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson speaks at an event in Delta on Oct. 18 announcing the party's new 'Thriving Kids' plan. B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson promises a fully costed party platform will be available later this afternoon (Sunday, Oct. 18). Doerkson was asked about the platform by a reporter at a media event held in Delta to announce the party’s “Thriving Kids Plan.” Doerkson was joined by Conservative candidates from around the region including Delta South’s Ian Paton – whose farm provided the backdrop for the event – and Delta North’s Monica Mohan. Also present were Surrey candidates Garry Thind (Surrey-Guildford), Mandeep Dhaliwal (Surrey North) and Bryan Tepper (Surrey Panorama), among others from the Lower Mainland. • a $500 activity credit – a refundable B.C. tax credit for sports, music, recreation and art camps; • support for families of children with autism, extending autism funding and reviewing changes by the BC NDP to ensure no family loses their funding. “Too many kids start the school day hungry. Too many families are working harder than ever and still can’t afford hockey, swimming, music, or summer camp. Too many schools have playgrounds that are falling apart, and parents spend years running bake sales to replace them. And too many classrooms have become a contest between the teacher and a cellular phone,” Doerkson said. “Here’s the truth: a child who is hungry, tired, restless, or distracted cannot learn. Every parent knows that. Every teacher sees the results.”

5ddba1385e099e656cfc9007b5758cc3.text: Green Party of Vancouver’s Pete Fry is the new mayor of B.C.’s largest city, Vancouver. Fry beat out incumbent Ken Sim, of ABC Vancouver, by more than 20,000 votes as of 11:20 p.m. on Saturday (Oct. 17). As of 11:20 p.m., Fry had 70,183. Sim had 49,780 votes. There had been 106 out of 149 polling locations counted at that point. Fry took to the stage for his winning speech shortly after 10:30 p.m. on Saturday (Oct. 17). At that time, 75 out of 149 polling locations had been counted. Sim made his concession speech shortly after. He was first elected in 2022, beating out incumbent Kennedy Stewart. Council is a mix of slates, with COPE, Green, OneCity and ABV Vancouver councillors. As of 11 p.m., in the lead is COPE’s Sean Orr (51,777), Green’s Annette Reilly (47,854), COPE’s Chloe Leslie (42,554), COPE’s Devyani Singh (41,031), OneCity’s Lucy Maloney (39,756), Green’s Stephanie Smith (38,498), COPE’s Solomon Yi-Kieran (38,013), Green’s Camil Dumont (37,514), ABC Vancouver’s Mike Klassen (36,927) and ABC Vancouver’s Joyce Gillespie (35,218).

2f218671ca8e24295761bba6b839d00d.text: Current RDOS Director Matt Taylor is throwing his hat into the ring to become Okanagan Falls' inaugural mayor. B.C.’s newest municipality has its first mayor. Matt Taylor has been elected mayor of the District of Okanagan Falls. According to Civic Info BC, Taylor received 780 votes to Tyler Johnsen’s 312 and Glen Innes’ 106. The Penticton Western spoke with Taylor shortly after he received the news himself. “I feel good,” said Taylor. “I think it was a decisive result, and I look forward to being able to benefit the community with having some experience in government.” Joining Taylor at the inaugural council table will be Amy Bydal, Allison Symons, Randy Ludwar and Eugene Dettling. A total of 1,207 ballots were cast in the election according to the preliminary results, out of a total eligible electorate of 2,360, which equates to about a 51 per cent turnout rate. “I would like to say thanks to the residents of Okanagan Falls for taking the time to show out in strong numbers for the vote,” said Taylor. ” I would like to say thanks for all the candidates, both at the mayor level and the councilor level, and the teams that worked with them, and obviously I’d like to thank my own supporters and my family for giving me the time.” Okanagan Falls’ residents voted in a 2025 referendum to incorporate as a municipality, the first to be established since 2016. The inaugural meeting of the District of Okanagan Falls’ new council will finish off the incorporation process on Nov. 6.

A familiar face is taking the reins in Quesnel as Coralee Oakes prepares to steer the city into its next chapter. Of the 7,806 estimated eligible voters in the Quesnel civic election, only 2,539 rose to the occasion and chose to keep a few familiar faces on council. Oakes won the mayoral race with 2,137 votes, defeating incumbent Ron Paull, who received 324 votes, according to results posted by Civic Info BC. The third mayoral candidate, Brian Waters, received 58 votes. Four incumbent city councillors were re-elected, with Mitch Vik receiving 1,066 votes, Scott Elliot earning 1,009, Tony Goulet securing 940 and Laurey-Anne Roodenburg receiving 890. Incumbents Debra McKelvie and Martin Runge did not receive enough votes to be re-elected, with 750 and 725 votes respectively. Newcomers Jeremy Drew and Ryan Adams also earned seats on council, receiving 1,281 and 809 votes, respectively. Drew received the highest vote total among the councillors listed. In an interview with the *Observer,* Oakes said the result came as a surprise and that she is grateful for the support from the community. “I want to recognize that I’m excited for an incredible team of councillors that have been elected. I think there is some great diversity, and I think we have a lot of work to do,” she said. “I very much look forward to getting to work with all of them soon.” According to Oakes, she connected with Ron Paull and thanked him for his many years of service. “I very much appreciate and I am grateful for all of the work that he has done,” she said. “I also wanted to recognize the important role that he’ll play in the upcoming 100th anniversary and so many exciting events that are going to be in the community.” Oakes also recognized all the other candidates that put their name forward for city council, regional district and school district. “We had absolutely top-notch people. c3852c91ac69d15a3117d3aa2b47f311.text: Jillian Merrick was elected mayor of Wells in the 2026 municipal election. Wells is turning a new page as Jillian Merrick takes the mayor’s chair, leading a council with three new faces. According to preliminary results shared by CivicInfo BC, Merrick won the mayoral race with 85 votes, defeating Rocky Nenka, who received 56 votes. Incumbent councillor Josh-Trotter Wanner was re-elected with 90 votes, while newcomers Miriam Dumitra, Elyssia Sasaki and Eric Andersen secured seats with 79, 76 and 70 votes, respectively.

119af2c4a3ffee2179ab44cfd1904ff0.text: Al Richmond is running for re-election as director of the Cariboo Regional District. Two of the three Cariboo Regional District directors from the South Cariboo retained their seats in the 2026 Municipal Elections. Incumbent director for Electoral Area H, Margo Wagner, and incumbent director for Area G, Al Richmond, both comfortably retained their seats. However, incumbent director for Area L, Eric de Vries, was defeated by challenger Dan Parker. Wagner received 81 per cent of the vote, with 229 of her constituents throwing their support behind her. Her challenger, John Kellett, received only 57 votes. Meanwhile, in the 108 Mile Ranch, Richmond received 641 votes, representing 68.9 per cent of the votes, while his challengers Michele Spence and Roz Griston received 255 votes and 35 votes, respectively. In Area L, the race was largely split between the four candidates, with Parker receiving exactly 33 per cent of the vote, or 286 ballots. Incumbent de Vries received 27.1 per cent of the votes, or 240 votes, followed closely by challenger McLean with 26.8 per cent, or 232 votes, while challenger Bo McKinney received 12.6 per cent, or 109 votes.

Owen Michael Torgerson, who ran uncontested for his third term as Mayor of Valemount, has been charged with sexual assault. Torgerson’s case came before Judge Cassandra Malfair in Prince George Provincial Court on Friday, Oct. 16. He was not there, but his lawyer, Jay Michi of Kamloops, appeared via videoconference on his behalf. Malfair agreed to Crown prosecutor Lisa Sukkau’s application for a publication ban to protect the identity of the woman who filed the criminal complaint against Torgerson. Torgerson’s next appearance, for arraignment, was scheduled for Oct. 29 in Valemount, but Malfair postponed it to Tuesday, Nov. 3 in Prince George, due to media attention to the case. The Tuesday, Oct. 13-sworn charge information sheet, signed by a justice of the peace, said an RCMP officer in Valemount has reasonable and probably grounds to believe that Torgerson committed sexual assault April 2 at or near Valemount. A notice on the Village of Valemount website said the Saturday, Oct. 17 municipal election was cancelled because all candidates for mayor and the four council seats had been elected by acclamation. On his X bio, the 1977-born Torgerson refers to himself as “On Leave Mayor of Valemount.” Under the NDP government’s amendments to the Community Charter, a member of a council is under mandatory leave of absence if charged under the Criminal Code “for a period that begins on the date of the charge, and ends” the day after the acquittal, discharge or withdrawal of the charge or on the date of conviction. Since Torgerson is innocent until proven guilty, he is not disqualified from being the mayor. “While on a leave of absence under this section, the council member continues to hold office but must not exercise a power or carry out a duty as a council member, and is entitled to remuneration and benefits to which the member would be entitled as a council member if the member were not on the leave of

The Social Planning Council continues to work on making a difference in Williams Lake and area through its poverty reduction strategy. At the latest regular city council meeting this month, Angelika Sellick presented an update on the Thrive Poverty Reduction Strategy and the work of the Poverty Reduction Working Group. The working group was formed in 2018 with the strategy that was endorsed by city council published in 2021 following extensive community consultation. “We all know the social planning council is in no way the only organization that is doing poverty reduction work in our community,” Sellick acknowledged, adding they recognize and celebrate the richness of organizations doing poverty reduction in their own communities without any direct connection to the Social Planning Council established in 1995. Through community consultation Sellick said the Social Planning Council has come to understand poverty as the condition in which people lack the resources, means, choices and opportunities to maintain self-sufficiency and a quality of life that supports basic needs, dignity and meaningful participation in the community. The Social Planning Council is a table that meets monthly to learn, share and collaborate on practical action and advocacy leading to increased community social well-being. Some organizations involved are the Salvation Army, Interior Health, Gibraltar Mine, the Foundry Cariboo Chilcotin, Women’s Contact Society, and WorkBC, in addition to representatives from city council. “Poverty is not the outcome of personal deficiencies or lack of will. It is the result of greater systemic failures,” Sellick said further noting poverty reduction work at the local level can contribute and lead to the ending of poverty at a global level. 59c0a5ade6c56c81de0d9e35ce7e6b34.text: B.C. Conservatives costed platform relies on economic growth that beats all forecasts | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. Conservatives costed platform relies on economic growth that beats all forecasts The B.C. Conservative Party released a fully costed platform on Sunday afternoon, projecting that under a Tory government, the deficit will fall from $13.7 billion this year to $10.8 billion by 2029, aided by the party’s forecast of spectacular 3.2 per cent economic growth. This assumes 2.5 per cent growth this year, 2.8 per cent next year, and 3.2 per cent in 2029 — growth levels far beyond most current economic forecasts. Ross Hickey, an associate professor of economics and management at UBC Okanagan, says this type of growth is unlikely. He gave a “cautiously optimistic” forecast of one per cent GDP growth per year for the next three years. The Bank of Canada projects national GDP growth at 0.7 per cent this year, 1.8 per cent next year, and 1.8 per cent the year after that. The Royal Bank of Canada projects B.C.’s economy to grow 0.8 per cent this year and 1.5 per cent next year. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says his party will achieve these higher levels by “supercharging” the economy. “We are predicting roughly one per cent more optimism in this province than the NDP,” Doerkson said Monday. “And frankly, I think it’s completely achievable.” But Doerkson fails to explain how some of his promises, such as ending Clean BC or reducing permitting times, will create the growth surge he promises. Hickey says words like “supercharge the economy” don’t say much, either. “There is a lot of rhetoric about what’s going to happen, that’s going to lead to growth, but it’s not a plan for how we’re going to get more growth,” he said. This type of growth would make B.C. a leader among advanced economies, which the International Monetary Fund projects will grow 2.1 per cent this year and 1.8 per cent next year, on average. The trial for Adam Troy Mann, who is accused of her murder, is underway in New Westminster Supreme Court. The man accused of stabbing and killing Surrey’s Tori Dunn in Port Kells on June 16, 2024 took the stand in New Westminster Supreme Court Monday. Adam Troy Mann, who was charged with second-degree murder in June of 2024, “is going to take the stand and he is going to give you his defence,” defence counsel Casey St. Germain told the jury in an opening statement. B.C. Supreme Court Justice David Layton is presiding over the trial, which started Oct. 5. St. Germain first asked Mann a little about himself. He turns 43 in December, and was born and raised in Windsor, Ont., court heard, with his mother and seven younger siblings. Mann, dressed in a dark sweatshirt and collared white shirt, sporting a full beard, remained standing while he testified, looking toward counsel as well as the jury and Dunn’s family members and friends who were present in the gallery. “My mother is black and my father is native,” Mann shared, saying his father left when he was a toddler, and his mother didn’t work, and was on welfare. “I grew up poor … (in) poverty,” Mann said, saying his father struggled with alcohol addiction. “He would become abusive (when he drank) and he would beat me and my other siblings,” Mann said, adding that it happened “every day.” He was placed in foster care around the age of five or six, he said, and started drinking “every day” around the age of 13 or 14. He didn’t finish high school, but went as far as Grade 10, court heard, and worked in construction sometimes. St. Germain asked him about his past criminal record, including a 2003 conviction in Ontario for possession of property obtained by crime, for which he served seven months, as well as a 2009 Ontario conviction for failure to comply with a court order. 77c8b180d6e84857b530587c33cb2bf0.text: Kent Rumbles was sentenced to four years in prison for a Nov. 6, 2021 head-on crash on the Bruhn Bridge at Sicamous that killed a Kamloops Shaun Stacey Michael. An Alberta man sentenced to four years jail time for a fatal collision in Sicamous has lost his court appeal. The collision occurred on the evening of Nov. 6, 2021, on the Bruhn Bridge where police found two pickup trucks had crashed head-on while crossing. The sole occupant of the eastbound truck, Kent Gordon Rumbles, was transported to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The driver of the westbound truck, a 48-year-old Shaun Stacey Michael of Kamloops, died at the scene. Police determined Rumbles’ vehicle had crossed the centre line. He was later charged and convicted of dangerous operation of a conveyance causing death, impaired operation of a conveyance causing death, and operating a conveyance with 80 milligrams of alcohol or more in 100 millilitres of blood causing death. In March 2025, Rumbles was sentenced to four years in prison. Later that month he was granted bail, having filed a notice of appeal. An appeal hearing was held on June 25, 2026, and on Oct. 16 Justice Karen Horsman released her decision: appeal dismissed. On the morning of Nov. 6, Rumbles left his home in Thorsby, Alta., driving to his seasonal property at Mabel Lake where he planned to meet his wife and mother-in-law. Horsman noted that other than taking a coffee to go, Rumbles, an insulin-dependent diabetic, “did not eat before leaving his house and he did not pack food for the trip.” “En route, the appellant stopped for gas. At that time, he purchased alcohol: a six-pack of White Claw hard seltzers, two bottles of wine, and a 750 ml bottle of raspberry vodka,” wrote Horsman in her reason for judgement. “As he continued driving, the appellant said he began to feel flu-like symptoms. 9a7e489f7350a02bb405aa78dd4cd028.text: CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko gestures during a B.C. election campaign stop in Surrey at Organic Warehouse, at 7093 King George Blvd. in Newton, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Affordability was the focus of another B.C. election campaign stop in Surrey for CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko on Monday morning, Oct. 19. The Surrey South candidate was at a Newton grocery store to reveal party plans “to put money back in British Columbians’ pockets, saving a typical two-income family approximately $540 a year.” Promised are lower taxes, a rate-of-inflation cap on residential BC Hydro rate increases, 20,000 new $10-a-day child care spaces by 2030 and a new refundable BC Commuter Credit to give passengers 15 per cent back on monthly/annual transit passes and BC Ferries multi-trip fares. If elected, CentreBC would reverse the NDP’s 2026 increase to the lowest provincial personal income tax bracket, reducing the rate to 5.06 per cent effective Jan. 1, 2027. Also, the renter’s tax credit will be increased to $600 a year and indexed to inflation. An existing freeze on ICBC basic insurance rates would be maintained until spring 2027, and rates would then be kept at or below inflation through 2030. “Our plan addresses household financial pressures together,” Sturko said at a podium set up in the produce section at Organic Warehouse. “People are working hard and still struggling to afford the basics,” said Sturko. “CentreBC will implement practical measures that lower household expenses, make bills more predictable and leave working families with more money in their pockets.” Sturko was named leader of CentreBC on Sept. 22 and announced her candidacy in Surrey South three days later. Many of the party’s campaign events have been held in Surrey, a key battleground in the B.C. election.
